promptText: A team adds four hand-picked few-shot examples to a support-ticket classification prompt, but all four examples happen to be long tickets. What is the most likely failure mode?
options: The model may overfit to the superficial 'long ticket' pattern rather than learning the actual classification rule the examples were meant to teach
Few-shot prompting can never underperform zero-shot, so no failure mode is possible here
The model will ignore the examples entirely because chat models cannot process more than one example at a time
Adding any examples always increases classification accuracy regardless of how they are chosen
explanation: Badly chosen few-shot examples that share an accidental superficial feature (like length) can cause the model to latch onto that spurious pattern instead of the actual task rule, which is why example selection and diversity matter as much as the decision to use few-shot at all.

promptText: Why can chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting actively hurt accuracy on some tasks rather than just adding unnecessary cost?
options: The model can talk itself into a plausible-sounding but incorrect reasoning chain and then confidently commit to the wrong final answer, which reads as more trustworthy than a terse wrong answer
CoT physically limits the model's context window so retrieved documents can no longer fit
CoT disables the model's ability to call tools or functions for the rest of the conversation
CoT always increases the temperature parameter, making outputs purely random
explanation: Beyond the extra latency and cost on tasks that don't need multi-step reasoning, CoT can actively hurt when the 'obvious' reasoning path is a well-known but wrong heuristic, producing a confident wrong answer that appears more credible than a blunt guess.

promptText: What is the key architectural reason prompt injection cannot be fully solved by prompting alone?
options: An LLM has no hard separation between instructions and data — everything in the context window is just tokens, so text that looks like an instruction may be followed regardless of its source
Prompt injection is purely a bug in specific model providers that will be patched in a future model release
Prompt injection only affects models that have not been fine-tuned on any safety data at all
The system message is cryptographically signed, so injected text can never override it
explanation: The root cause is architectural: instructions and data share the same token stream, so any untrusted text inserted into the prompt (user input, retrieved documents, tool output) is a potential injection vector that no amount of prompt wording can fully close off.

promptText: A model uses schema-constrained decoding (strict function-calling) so its output is guaranteed to be syntactically valid JSON matching the schema. What does this guarantee NOT cover?
options: That the values placed in the fields are factually or semantically correct — the model can still populate a well-typed field with a wrong value
That the output will parse as JSON at all
That required fields will be present in the output
That enum fields will only contain one of the allowed values
explanation: Schema-constrained decoding guarantees structural/syntactic validity by construction, but it says nothing about semantic correctness — the model can still put a wrong-but-well-typed value in a field, so business-rule validation is still required.

promptText: Why is cosine similarity generally preferred over Euclidean distance for comparing text embeddings of documents with very different lengths?
options: Cosine similarity measures only the angle between vectors and ignores magnitude, so it isn't skewed by the different vector lengths that can result from documents of different sizes
Euclidean distance cannot be computed on vectors with more than 512 dimensions
Cosine similarity is always faster to compute than any other distance metric on any hardware
Euclidean distance only works for sparse vectors, never for dense embeddings
explanation: Cosine similarity ignores vector magnitude and captures only direction/orientation, which is why it is robust to magnitude differences that can arise from documents of varying length, unlike Euclidean distance which is sensitive to absolute position and scale.

promptText: A query containing the exact error code 'ERR_CONN_4042' returns poor results from a pure dense (embedding-based) retrieval system. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The embedding model may lack a strong learned representation for the rare exact token, so it matches on generic semantic context instead of the precise literal string
Dense retrieval cannot process queries containing numbers under any circumstances
The vector database's ANN index has a hard limit on query string length that was exceeded
Dense embeddings only work for single-word queries, never multi-token strings
explanation: Dense retrieval's core weakness is exact-term blindness on rare tokens like error codes or SKUs, because the embedding model may not have learned a strong distinction for that token and instead relies on general semantic similarity — exactly the failure mode that motivates hybrid search with sparse/BM25 retrieval.

promptText: A team upgrades to a newer embedding model but, to save cost, only re-embeds new documents going forward while leaving the historical corpus on the old vectors. What happens?
options: Retrieval quality degrades unpredictably because queries embedded with the new model are being compared against a mixed index of vectors from two different, incompatible geometric spaces
Nothing changes, because all embedding models share the same universal coordinate system
The vector database automatically detects and re-normalizes vectors from different models on the fly
Only the newly added documents become unsearchable, while old documents continue to retrieve normally
explanation: Embedding drift means vectors from different models are not comparable — there is no shared coordinate system, so a mixed index of old and new vectors silently returns nonsense for whichever half doesn't match the query's embedding space, requiring a full re-embed rather than incremental migration.

promptText: A product-documentation RAG system using naive fixed-size chunking (500 tokens, no overlap) splits a numbered installation procedure so that step 4's instructions land in one chunk and its prerequisite warning lands in the next. What chunking approach directly addresses this failure?
options: Structure-aware (semantic) chunking that respects document boundaries like headers and keeps each documented procedure intact as one chunk, up to a size cap
Reducing the fixed chunk size to 100 tokens so warnings are more likely to be isolated in their own chunk
Switching from cosine similarity to Euclidean distance in the vector search
Increasing the embedding dimensionality so more semantic nuance is captured per chunk
explanation: Semantic/structure-aware chunking splits at natural meaning boundaries (headers, paragraphs, procedure boundaries) rather than an arbitrary token count, keeping a coherent unit like a full procedure together instead of severing it mid-step.

promptText: Why does hybrid search typically combine dense and sparse retrieval results using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) rather than simply averaging their raw similarity scores?
options: BM25 scores and cosine-similarity scores are on entirely different, incomparable scales, so RRF sidesteps that problem by combining results based only on each document's rank in each list
RRF is required because vector databases cannot return numeric similarity scores, only rankings
Averaging scores is computationally impossible at query time due to floating-point precision limits
RRF eliminates the need to run sparse retrieval at all, using only the dense results
explanation: A BM25 score and a cosine-similarity score cannot be meaningfully averaged because they live on different scales; RRF instead fuses results purely by rank position within each method's list, which works regardless of how the underlying scores are distributed.

promptText: Why does a two-stage retrieval funnel (fast initial retrieval of the top 50-100 chunks, followed by a cross-encoder reranker narrowing to the top 5) outperform running the reranker over the entire corpus directly?
options: A cross-encoder jointly processes the query and each candidate together, which is far more accurate but too expensive to run against millions of chunks, so it's reserved for the small candidate set that survives cheap initial retrieval
Cross-encoders can only process exactly 50 documents at a time due to a hard architectural limit
Running a reranker over the full corpus would produce identical results to running it on a candidate set, so the two-stage design is purely a legacy convention
Initial retrieval and reranking must use the same embedding model, so a full-corpus rerank is mathematically impossible
explanation: A cross-encoder models fine-grained query-document interactions jointly, which is fundamentally more accurate but too slow/expensive to run at corpus scale, which is why cheap-and-broad initial retrieval followed by expensive-and-narrow reranking is what makes accurate retrieval affordable.

promptText: In a multi-tenant RAG system with fine-grained access control, why is 'post-filtering' (running similarity search first, then discarding results that fail a metadata permission check) dangerous?
options: If the permission condition excludes most of the corpus, the top-K similarity results might all get filtered out, leaving too few or zero results even though relevant, permitted documents exist further down the unfiltered ranking
Post-filtering is always faster than pre-filtering, so it introduces no correctness risk, only a minor performance cost
Post-filtering permanently deletes documents from the vector index instead of just excluding them from one query's results
Metadata filtering cannot technically be applied after a similarity search has already returned results
explanation: When a permission filter is narrow, the top-K similarity results computed before filtering may all be filtered out, silently starving the user of relevant content that exists further down the ranking — pre-filtering or ANN-integrated filtering avoids this failure mode.

promptText: An evaluation set shows Recall@20 at 94% but Recall@5 at only 61% for a RAG pipeline. What does this specific gap indicate, and what is the appropriate fix?
options: The relevant content is almost always findable in the corpus but is being ranked too low to reach the small top-5 slice sent to the LLM — a ranking problem best fixed by adding a reranking stage
The embedding model has failed to index roughly a third of the corpus and needs to be fully retrained
The vector database's ANN index is corrupted and needs to be rebuilt from scratch
This gap is expected behavior and indicates no problem in the retrieval pipeline at all
explanation: A high Recall@20 with a much lower Recall@5 shows retrieval coverage is fine (the right chunk is usually somewhere in the corpus) but ranking is poor (it isn't reaching the small final slice), which points specifically to a reranking/scoring fix rather than a coverage or embedding-model problem.

promptText: A financial-summary assistant's retrieval-only evaluation shows it almost always fetches the correct source documents, yet a manual audit finds 1 in 12 answers contain a subtly wrong number (attributing one quarter's figure to a different quarter). Which combination of diagnosis and fix is correct?
options: This is a generation-side faithfulness failure invisible to retrieval metrics alone; it requires a separate faithfulness check (e.g., an LLM-as-judge verifying each claim is entailed by the retrieved context) rather than tuning retrieval further
This proves retrieval is actually broken despite what the retrieval-only evaluation showed, so the fix is to increase top-K and add more chunk overlap
This is caused by using dot product instead of cosine similarity, and switching distance metrics will resolve the number confusion
This indicates the embedding model is stale and needs an immediate re-embedding migration of the entire corpus
explanation: Retrieval quality and generation faithfulness are separate failure modes: here retrieval is confirmed healthy, so the wrong numbers are a generation-side conflation error, which can only be caught and fixed by evaluating faithfulness of the final answer against retrieved context directly, not by tuning the retrieval stage.

promptText: A RAG pipeline retrieves the single correct chunk reliably, but final answers are still frequently wrong. Debugging reveals the correct chunk is present in the assembled prompt but is positioned in the middle of eight other chunks. Which combination of concepts explains this and the most appropriate mitigation?
options: This is the lost-in-the-middle effect, where models attend less reliably to content buried in the middle of a long context; mitigating it means keeping the retrieved set small and high-precision (via reranking) and deliberately positioning the highest-confidence chunk near the start or end
This is an embedding drift problem, and the fix is to re-embed the entire corpus with a newer model version
This is a prompt-injection attack originating from one of the other eight chunks, and the fix is stricter input sanitization
This means Recall@K is too low, and the only fix is to increase K further so more chunks are retrieved
explanation: Lost-in-the-middle means position within the context — not just presence — affects whether the model actually uses a chunk; the fix is a smaller, higher-precision retrieved set (via reranking) plus deliberate ordering, since simply retrieving the right chunk is not sufficient if it's buried among many others.

promptText: A team serving tens of millions of chunks is deciding between a 3072-dimension and a 768-dimension embedding model, and separately whether they need a dedicated vector database at all. Which reasoning correctly connects these two decisions?
options: Higher dimensionality directly multiplies storage, comparison cost, and ANN index size, so at tens of millions of vectors the dimensionality choice can be the difference between an index fitting in memory on one machine versus needing distributed infrastructure — exactly the scale threshold where a dedicated vector database becomes justified rather than premature
Embedding dimensionality and vector database choice are entirely unrelated decisions with no shared cost driver
A dedicated vector database is required at any scale specifically because brute-force search cannot run in memory regardless of dimensionality
Lower-dimension embeddings always produce strictly worse retrieval quality, so the 768-dimension option should never be considered regardless of cost
explanation: Dimensionality is a direct multiplier on storage and ANN index cost, and at large corpus scale this compounds with the decision of whether brute-force in-memory search suffices or a dedicated, possibly distributed vector database is justified — the two decisions share the same underlying cost driver: total vector footprint at scale.
